stories.headline: Denver moves to shut down Five Points nightclub after security guard accused of sexual assault at gunpoint
stories.summary:
Denver licensing officials issued a summary suspension Tuesday ordering the Olympus Discotheque at 2036 N. Broadway to cease operations immediately, citing a July 18 attack in which an unlicensed security guard allegedly kidnapped and sexually assaulted an 18-year-old patron at gunpoint inside the club after closing time. The guard, 37-year-old Vincente David Espino-Gonzalez, is accused of holding the woman for approximately an hour in an assault largely captured on the club's surveillance cameras before she escaped and flagged down a passing police officer.

Espino-Gonzalez was identified as the owner of Sparta Security & Consulting Services, whose city license expired in 2024, and he was not licensed as a security guard. City officials also cited a July 24 undercover operation in which an underage police cadet entered the club and purchased three alcoholic drinks without challenge.

Summary suspensions are an emergency licensing measure used in response to immediate threats to public health and safety and are historically rare. The city has issued three such suspensions this year, including one against another Denver nightclub following a shooting that killed one person and wounded eight others. Club owner Wuilmer Varela Cardoza declined to comment except to say there is 'a lot of false information out there' and that he is preparing for an Aug. 18 hearing to challenge the suspension.

stories.headline: CU Denver closes on $27.95 million purchase of Independence Plaza tower downtown
stories.summary:
The University of Colorado Denver has completed the acquisition of Independence Plaza, a 25-story, 567,000-square-foot office tower at 1050 17th St. in downtown Denver, purchasing it Monday for just under $28 million — roughly $2 million less than the price approved by the Board of Regents in June. The sale price represents an approximately 80 percent discount from the building's last sale in 2007, when it fetched $144.5 million.

CU Denver plans to occupy about 200,000 square feet of the tower, which is currently only 21 percent occupied. The remainder of the office space will be leased to companies and startups, some of which will be housed in an innovation and entrepreneurship hub; the Denver Downtown Development Authority awarded CU a $4.5 million grant in July to help establish that hub.

The acquisition pushes CU Denver's campus presence from the Auraria campus on downtown's periphery directly into the city core along the renovated 16th Street corridor. City and downtown leaders called the purchase a significant step in efforts to revitalize downtown by diversifying its economic base beyond traditional office tenants. University officials said it could take months before students begin using the building.

stories.headline: New Colorado rideshare safety law takes effect, requiring faster investigation of driver complaints
stories.summary:
A new Colorado law went into effect Wednesday requiring Uber, Lyft and other rideshare companies to investigate driver complaints — including those involving sexual assault, harassment and stalking — within seven business days or face penalties. House Bill 1424, the Colorado Rideshare Safety and Accountability Act, also mandates that a human reviewer, not an algorithm, handle complaint investigations.

The legislation was co-sponsored by state Rep. Jenny Willford, who disclosed at the start of the 2025 legislative session that a Lyft driver sexually assaulted her in February 2024. In that case, the driver turned out to be a different person than the one listed on the Lyft app, having accessed and impersonated another driver's account; Willford later sued both Lyft and the transportation company involved.

The new law also includes provisions aimed at preventing drivers who use imposter, shared or rented accounts from continuing to operate on rideshare platforms. Uber has faced thousands of lawsuits nationally alleging failures to implement appropriate safety measures; a New York Times investigation found the company received more than 400,000 reports of sexual assault or misconduct between 2017 and 2022.

stories.headline: New Colorado law speeds up missing college student response, inspired by death of CU student Megan Trussell
stories.summary:
A new Colorado law took effect Wednesday requiring law enforcement officers to have specific training on missing person alerts and mandating that colleges and universities conduct a 'Preliminary Wellness Assessment' if a student is reported missing. Under SB26-120, schools must also contact law enforcement immediately if there is a credible risk to a student's safety or if the student has been missing more than six hours.

The law was championed by the family of Megan Trussell, a University of Colorado student who disappeared in February 2025 and was found dead days later. Her parents said one of their most frustrating experiences was getting authorities to take the disappearance seriously in its early hours. State Sen. Janice Marchman, a Democrat representing Boulder and Larimer counties, was the prime sponsor of the legislation.

Another case also shaped the bill: Kaylee Russell, who went missing late in 2025, was not the subject of a missing person alert until days after she was last seen; she was later found dead in a canal in what investigators said was a single-vehicle crash. Denver7 contacted major Colorado universities to assess their compliance with the new requirements.

stories.headline: Denver Water begins issuing fines for violations of mandatory water use restrictions
stories.summary:
Denver Water has begun levying fines against metro-area customers who are not complying with mandatory water use restrictions currently in effect. Officials have described the penalties as significant in size, though specific fine amounts were not detailed in available reporting.

The enforcement action marks an escalation in the utility's efforts to enforce conservation measures across its service area. Mandatory restrictions were put in place to manage water supplies amid ongoing drought and high-demand summer conditions.

Denver Water serves approximately 1.5 million people across the Denver metro area. Customers found to be violating watering schedules or other restriction requirements are subject to the new fines.

stories.headline: Broncos hold third public open house on Burnham Yard stadium district plan
stories.summary:
Denver Broncos officials, city planners and neighborhood residents gathered Wednesday at La Alma Recreation Center for the third public open house on the Burnham Yard small area plan, a key step in the team's effort to develop a new stadium district on the former rail yard south of downtown. Broncos President Damani Leech told attendees the master plan is built around four priorities: integrating the new district with surrounding neighborhoods, honoring the site's rail history, improving mobility through the area, and creating lasting economic opportunity.

The Broncos this week acquired land from SRM Concrete covering nearly 10 acres on the northern portion of the proposed district, and last week released new renderings of the project. Owner and CEO Greg Penner said Tuesday there are 'a lot of moving pieces' to work through before a spring 2027 construction start date can be targeted.

Community members at the meeting used interactive stations to weigh in on priorities including affordable housing, industrial land-use regulations, public art, retail development and pedestrian mobility. City planners expect to release a public review draft of the Burnham Yard Small Area Plan in October, with final adoption anticipated by year-end following additional public feedback and City Council review.

stories.headline: Nuggets decline Jalen Pickett's team option, lower asking price on Peyton Watson sign-and-trade
stories.summary:
The Denver Nuggets have chosen not to exercise Jalen Pickett's team option, according to a report from The Denver Post, making the guard an unrestricted free agent. The decision removes Pickett from the team's roster heading into the 2026-27 season.

Separately, ESPN's Shams Charania reported that the Nuggets have lowered their asking price in a potential sign-and-trade involving restricted free agent wing Peyton Watson, a sign the team is motivated to find a deal for the young forward. Watson was a key reserve contributor during Denver's recent playoff runs.

The Nuggets also agreed to a one-year, $3.3 million deal with Lonnie Walker IV, completing his NBA comeback after he was granted an early exit from a contract with Maccabi Tel Aviv. In addition, Denver will hire Dave Joerger as top assistant coach under head coach David Adelman, according to Charania.

stories.headline: Rockies rally past Diamondbacks 3-2 as Zac Veen homers in first start back from Triple-A
stories.summary:
The Colorado Rockies defeated the Arizona Diamondbacks 3-2 Tuesday night in Phoenix behind a strong outing from Tomoyuki Sugano, who threw six solid innings. Kyle Karros hit a two-run homer but left the game after a collision with a teammate.

Zac Veen, recalled from Triple-A following a standout stretch in the minors, made an immediate impact in his first start back, hitting a two-run homer to help power the Rockies' offense. The win provided some relief for a Colorado club that has been hovering near the worst record in the major leagues.

The Rockies had previously topped the Boston Red Sox 3-2 on a Jake McCarthy three-run triple in the ninth inning. Colorado's recent results offer a modest uptick for a team that has struggled throughout the 2026 season.

stories.headline: National CineMedia strikes $275 million deal to acquire Captivate, stock drops sharply
stories.summary:
Centennial-based National CineMedia has agreed to acquire Captivate Holdings for $275 million, expanding the company's digital advertising platform beyond movie theaters and into office buildings and residential properties. National CineMedia is one of the largest cinema advertising networks in the United States.

The deal is intended to diversify NCM's revenue streams by giving it access to Captivate's network of screens in workplaces and residential buildings, reducing its dependence on theatrical advertising tied to film attendance. However, investors reacted negatively to the announcement, with the company's stock falling sharply following the news.

National CineMedia has its headquarters in Centennial, Colorado, making the deal a significant development for a major local corporation. The company has navigated a challenging environment for cinema advertising in recent years as streaming competition has altered moviegoing habits.

stories.headline: Denver distressed property owners push back against investor's legal tactics to acquire neglected buildings
stories.summary:
Some owners of properties on Denver's neglected and derelict building list are objecting to the tactics of local investor John Crays, who has used creative legal maneuvers to pry problem properties from their owners — in some cases acquiring them at auction. Crays has been convincing neighboring landowners to assign him their private rights of action, then suing owners of neglected homes to have court-ordered caretakers appointed and properties auctioned.

Denver's neglected and derelict building list, updated last month, contains 310 buildings across the city. To qualify, a property generally must be unoccupied, unsafe or a nuisance, habitually in code violation, or at least a year behind on property taxes. The city can issue fines for non-compliance with registration requirements, yet many properties remain on the list year after year.

Some affected owners say they are actively working to rehabilitate their properties but lack the financial resources to do so quickly. Among them is Justine Sandoval, an organizer running for Colorado House District 5, whose family has held a Curtis Park home for four generations. While some neighbors have praised Crays for dealing with blight, others say the approach fails to account for owners who are genuinely trying to save their properties.

stories.headline: Colorado mountain real estate bounces back in July after snowless winter dampened sales
stories.summary:
Real estate agents in Colorado's mountain communities are reporting improved market conditions after a difficult winter season that saw record-low snowpack and an early closure at Mary Jane Mountain in Winter Park. Grand County, located about 60 miles west of Denver, was among the hardest hit, but agents say July numbers have recovered meaningfully.

The broader Colorado housing market showed mixed signals in July, with fewer pending contracts statewide than a year ago (7,599 vs. 7,624) and the median days on market creeping up from 55 to 58 days. A growing divide emerged between single-family homes, which held their prices, and multifamily properties such as condos and townhomes, which faced weaker demand and softer pricing; the statewide median multifamily sale price dipped to $397,250 from $400,000 a year earlier.

In Winter Park, by contrast, homes averaged just 28 days on market in July, and high-end resort properties are moving briskly. The Denver Parade of Homes is currently featuring resort homes in Winter Park and Fraser, with prices ranging from $1.235 million for a townhouse to nearly $3 million for larger single-family cabins — including a full cul-de-sac of homes in Koelbel's Rendezvous development that has sold out.

topStory.headline: Karoline Leavitt to Leave White House Press Secretary Role at End of August
topStory.summary:
White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt will step down from her position at the end of August, President Donald Trump announced Wednesday on his Truth Social platform. Trump said Leavitt, 28, is departing "so she can spend more time with her beautiful young children and family" and that she will become "one of my top outside advisors" and "an influential voice within the Republican Party."

Leavitt confirmed her departure in a statement posted to X, saying the role has been "the honor and adventure of a lifetime" but that since returning from maternity leave she has felt she "cannot be the best mom my two young children deserve while devoting the constant time, energy, and attention required of the White House Press Secretary." She gave birth to her second child, a daughter named Viviana, in May, becoming the first White House press secretary to have a child while serving in the role, and returned to the briefing room podium on July 16. Neither Trump nor Leavitt indicated who might succeed her in the position.

Leavitt became the youngest person ever to serve as White House press secretary when Trump returned to office in January 2025, surpassing Ronald Ziegler, who was 29 when he held the role under President Richard Nixon. She previously served as an assistant press secretary during Trump's first term and as his national press secretary during the 2024 presidential campaign, during which she gave birth to her first child and returned to work after just four days when an assassination attempt was made against Trump in Butler, Pennsylvania. She also ran unsuccessfully as the Republican nominee for New Hampshire's first congressional district in 2022.

Leavitt's tenure of roughly 18 months ranks as the second-longest for a Trump White House press secretary, behind Sarah Huckabee Sanders, who served nearly two years during the first term. She is the fifth woman in a high-ranking position to leave the Trump administration this year, following Attorney General Pam Bondi, Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, Labor Secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer, and Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard, all of whom were replaced by men. During her absence on maternity leave earlier this year, the White House declined to name an interim press secretary, instead deploying senior officials including Vice President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to brief reporters.
